newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: NATIONAL PARTY MP HAS ADVICE FOR PARTY LEADERSHIP
Federal National Party M-P, Ian Causley, has urged party leader, Tim Fischer, to get closer to his constituency and present its views more strongly in the public arena.
Mr Causley is warning the Government's decision to freeze tariffs in the car industry, when the sugar tariff is about to be abolished, could affect support for the Coalition.
Sugar growers and two National M-Ps, De-Anne Kelly and Bob Katter, have already expressed anger at the decision.
Mr Causley has told A-B-C Radio, there is a concern among rural voters that while they are leading the way on tariff cuts, other industries are reluctant to follow.
He says this could also have implications for Tim Fischer's leadership.
NEW ASSAULT ON PROPOSALS TO MINE URANIUM NEAR KAKADU

The Australian Conservation Foundation says uranium mining near Kakadu National Park in the Northern Territory, would see a reduction of the values that have lifted the Park into World Heritage listing.
Conservationists want the Prime Minister to reject the proposed Jabiluka uranium mine.
The call comes on the day the final Environmental Impact Statement for the project is expected to be forwarded to the Federal Government.
The A-C-F's Dave Sweeney says John Howard needs to recognise the widespread community opposition to uranium mining alongside Kakadu National Park.
A rally against the Jabiluka mine is planned for five o'clock this afternoon at Civic Park in central Darwin.
ORPHAN BABIES USED TO TEST HERPES VACCINE
Scientists say children in Melbourne orphanages who were used as human guinea pigs to test new vaccines and antibiotics between 1945 and 1970 were only given harmless injections.
The Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research says there were no deaths from the tests.
The institute's Dr David Vaux, says at least 16 babies at the Broadmeadows Babies' Home were injected with an experimental vaccine against the herpes simplex virus.
Dr Vaux says it would have been wrong not to try to protect the babies from the disease.
He says they would have suffered only slight side-effects, like soreness at the injection point, and some vomiting.
Dr Vaux says permission to undertake the tests would have come from the Sisters of Saint Joseph, who ran the orphanage.
BANK HOTLINE OPEN TODAY IN NSW
Bank customers throughout New South Wales have been invited to lodge their concerns today about banking services on a free-call hotline.
The line will be open between nine o'clock and five o'clock. The number is 1800-064-499.
The Council of Social Service has set up the hotline amid increasing concerns over the negative impacts the activities of some banks are having on rural communities and the disadvantaged.
Council director Gary Moore says while banking is a private market service, it is also an essential service for all citizens.
Mr Moore is encouraging callers to make suggestions for improvements to banking services.
The hotline findings will be presented to a banking industry forum next month.

OPPOSITION SIEZES ON NATIONAL PARTY DISSENT ON SUGAR TARIFFS The Federal Opposition is trying to capitalise on National Party dissent on sugar tariffs, by calling for a formal vote on the issue in Parliament.
National Party MP's Deanne Kelly and Bob Katter have criticised the decision to freeze car tariffs, but abolish tariffs on sugar, saying it shows the government favours the cities over the bush.
Shadow Industry spokesman, Simon Crean, says legislation should be used to ensure a full debate and vote in the Parliament.
Mr Crean says any members of the National Party who disagree with the Government's decision should be given the chance to cross the floor.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
